chunks.text: Sterculia foetida — called Java olive, skunk tree, bastard poon tree or wild almond depending on region — is a large, soft-wooded, dioecious deciduous tree native across the Indian subcontinent, Indo-China and parts of Malesia (including the Philippines and Sumatra), and since introduced to places as far-flung as the Gulf of Guinea islands, Hainan and several Caribbean islands. It can grow to around 35 metres, with branches arranged in distinctive horizontal whorls, smooth grey bark with a fibrous inner layer, and large palmately compound leaves of 7–9 leaflets clustered at branch tips. Its bell-shaped, five-lobed flowers turn from yellowish-green to deep red as they age and are notoriously foul-smelling — plant explorer David Fairchild reportedly considered it the worst-smelling flower he ever encountered — which, along with the genus name's link to Sterquilinus, the Roman god of manure, explains the common name 'skunk tree.' The woody, bright-red, star-shaped fruit splits into several follicles, each lined with stinging bristles and holding roughly 10–15 blue-black seeds; these seeds are edible once roasted (raw seeds are considered unsafe) and the extracted oil has been evaluated as a potential biodiesel feedstock, with flash point, iodine value and viscosity reportedly falling within ASTM and EN biodiesel specifications. A notable caution: the tree's cyclopropene fatty acids, including sterculic acid, have been flagged in toxicology literature as carcinogenic or co-carcinogenic in animal studies, a point Wikipedia itself tags as needing stronger citation but worth treating seriously before recommending casual consumption of any part of the plant.

chunks.source: Singapore National Parks Board — FloraFauna Web, Sterculia foetida
chunks.text: NParks' Singapore profile largely corroborates the Wikipedia description — a large deciduous tree to about 40 metres with whorled, horizontal branches, palmately compound leaves of 5–9 leaflets, and dioecious, foul-smelling, red-calyxed flowers — while adding useful local context: two individual Sterculia foetida trees at the Singapore Botanic Gardens have been designated Heritage Trees, reflecting the species' long history and civic value as a shade and avenue tree in tropical city planting, despite its size making it best suited to parks and open spaces rather than small gardens. The page lists the bright red, ellipsoid follicles as the tree's chief ornamental feature, and confirms several of the same practical uses noted elsewhere: the seeds are edible, the easily-worked but not especially durable timber has traditionally been used for items like canoes and hut doors, bark fibres can be twisted into rope, and the leaves serve as fodder. It also flags a regional pest concern — the leaf-rolling insect Sylepta balteata is considered a serious pest of the tree in India — and notes the seeds have a notably long storage shelf life, which supports easy propagation by seed. Interestingly, the same page both lists the flowers as a 'fragrant' ornamental feature and separately describes them as foul-smelling, a contradiction likely owing to subjective perception of the scent, and a detail worth flagging rather than resolving one way or the other.
